content: Ensuring the availability of high-quality and comparable data is essential for global monitoring of HIV programs. The recommended indicators for national HIV programs cover the entire care cascade, emphasizing critical aspects of service coverage and quality. These indicators align with international strategic, programmatic, and clinical priorities, focusing on outcomes and impact. They serve as the foundation for routine data reviews to enhance program performance at national, district, and facility levels. Key national HIV program indicators include: Reducing the number of individuals at substantial risk of acquiring HIV. Ensuring 95% of people living with HIV know their status and are linked to treatment. Achieving 95% antiretroviral therapy (ART) coverage among people living with HIV, with 95% of those on ART achieving viral suppression. Reducing mortality associated with tuberculosis (TB). Decreasing the number of children acquiring HIV. Reducing comorbidities and mortality related to sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Detailed indicator tables for each program area, spanning testing, treatment, and care, are available in the 2020 WHO Consolidated HIV Strategic Information Guidelines. Disaggregating data by geographical and sociodemographic subpopulations is a core component of cascade analysis. This approach allows program managers to address performance and equity issues in access and service quality. Identifying and addressing barriers for underserved groups is the fastest way to achieve overall program targets. Disaggregated analysis highlights gaps in service delivery for specific groups, such as pregnant women or individuals with both TB and HIV, enabling tailored management and services. Routine assessments of equity in service delivery and quality across groups are fundamental to tracking these commitments. All collected data must be treated as confidential, particularly for key populations facing stigma and discrimination. Data should be securely stored, and staff must be trained to maintain patient confidentiality. Strengthening data systems is critical as countries plan investments in their health information systems. Sustainable strategic information systems for HIV must align with broader health information systems as part of an integrated architecture. Guidance on national health information system standards, policies, and tools is available to support the development of appropriate systems, including digital health strategies and interoperability models. Most countries manage complex systems of individual patient-level and aggregated data. Patient information systems often interface with laboratory and pharmacy systems to capture essential data for cascade analysis, validation, and quality assessment. However, variations in data systems arise from differences in local infrastructure, digital health leadership, and resource investments. Harmonizing disparate reporting methods is crucial for comprehensive program performance assessments. Effective monitoring and management also require data from community-based services, which are vital for high-risk populations who may not seek services at health facilities. Data systems must increasingly integrate information from community-based services, such as mobile clinics and outreach workers, to address gaps in understanding service coverage and quality for these populations. National HIV monitoring and evaluation frameworks should incorporate data from multiple sources for use at different management levels. Core data elements in primary collection tools often serve multiple purposes, including patient care, program management, and monitoring. Monitoring ART program functioning involves assessing each stage of the testing, prevention, and treatment cascade to identify progress, gaps, and trends in incidence and mortality. Regular program reviews should evaluate these stages to improve outcomes. For example, monitoring ARV drug toxicity is essential, particularly with the transition to dolutegravir (DTG) as the preferred first-line ART. Routine monitoring of treatment-limiting toxicity, defined as life-threatening illness, hospitalization, or serious adverse drug reactions, is recommended to inform national guidelines and prevent toxicity. Longitudinal monitoring is also encouraged to address emerging concerns, such as weight gain associated with DTG use. This involves tracking changes in body weight, metabolic comorbidities, and cardiovascular risks over time. Such monitoring complements adverse drug reaction reporting and provides insights into temporal patterns of toxicity and risk factors among people living with HIV. Global surveillance of ARV drug safety is critical, particularly for new drugs and in pregnancy. WHO has developed a central database to pool safety data from countries, enabling rapid evidence generation and detection of toxicity signals. Surveillance of HIV drug resistance is also a global priority, as resistance to non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NNRTIs) and nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors (NRTIs) threatens ART effectiveness. WHO recommends transitioning to DTG-based first-line ART regimens in response to rising NNRTI resistance. Surveillance of resistance among children is also critical, as high levels of pretreatment resistance have been observed in infants newly diagnosed with HIV. This underscores the need for child-friendly, non-NNRTI-based ART formulations and rational sequencing of ARV regimens. To address HIV drug resistance, WHO recommends that countries develop national action plans integrated into their HIV strategic plans. These plans should include high-impact interventions to prevent and respond to resistance, quality-of-care monitoring, and periodic surveys of resistance among various populations. Surveillance data should inform optimal ART regimen selection and national guidelines. In summary, robust data systems, routine monitoring, and targeted interventions are essential for improving HIV program outcomes, addressing drug resistance, and ensuring equitable access to high-quality services.
